name: Plot_79au_First_Approach
title: The Object at 79au
desc:
At long last, you approach the location of your many visions.

Before you you see an enormous golden sphere. While it's the size of a large asteroid, you're certain it is not a natural formation. As you stare at the strange object, you find your senses stunned and your reason stupified. Who could have built such a thing? And why?

You find yourself compelled to get closer to the surface of the object. To touch it's surface. But you feel equally a palpable dread, a stupifying fear of the unknown and impossible.

name: Plot_79au_Spacewalk
title: Spacewalk To The Interface
desc:
You spacewalk to the object, feeling an ever growing sense of terror the closer you get. 

The surface is a gossamer knit weave of golden threads pulled taut and rigid to the touch. Above you is a platform sticking out of the sphere, the only irregularity to the curve of the object. 

You float to it and see a strange interface above the platform. A hexagonal pillar beside a hexagonal hole. You take the pillar from the surface and hold it in your hand.

name: Plot_79au_Leave
title: Leave The Object Be
desc: Overwhelmed by terror, you decide to leave the strange object. For now.

name: Plot_79au_Pillar
title: Insert the Pillar
desc:
The golden weave loosens before you and begins to open. The hole before you reveals a bright purple light, and as it grows larger you see there is a shimmering liquid inside of the same color. The opening grows and grows, eventually becomes as large as your ship.

You have a vision of an infinite plane suddenly pockmarked with other purple nodes in a network, of which this is just one. You feel a sublime expansive terror, as if you are an ant on an anthill and the camera zooms out and you realize your world is tiny in comparison.
 
You have a terrrible certainty that suddenly you are being observed by trillions of eyes, and most of them are curious. Many of them are coming. Very soon. Perhaps now.

name: Plot_79au_Enter
title: Enter the Sphere
desc:
Following a feeling of naive optimism and a willingness to risk one's own life, you enter the sphere. You know that humanity is flawed, failing, but has an ineffable essence that should expand and continue. Going through, even if it kills you personally, is worth it.
 
You find yourself in a bureaucratic metaphysical switchboard  in which you must imagine your ship's essence.

You blink to ... somewhere? Silence. You hear your ship nav pan sound but it is panning like crazy, faster and faster as it scrolls out to your new location, lightyears away.

name: Plot_79au_Others
title: Let the Others Arrive
desc:
Following a perfectly rational pessimism and a drive to protect one's own life, you wait and see who arrives. You're certain Humanity is failing itself. It can no longer be trusted to decide its own fate. Anything coming through must be better than what we got. Let Daddy come home and sort it out for us. 

The Entity comes through and asks you "Are you Merga?" Before you can answer, and without any emotion, The Entity harvests all of humanity in the blink of an eye. You enter a dead system as the only remaining human in the universe.

name: 79AU_Approach20
title: 20 AU
desc:
The Object grows larger in your scope with each passing day.

You find yourself watching it for hours. You studied the readouts, the videos, the decades of identical reports made by astronomers assigned to observe it. Those methods became insufficient. 

The optics suite has an eyepiece which, when you look through it, is as close as possible to the unfiltered image captured in the hull-mounted scopes. You keep your eye fixed to that scope until you fall asleep in your chair, and then you watch it in your dreams.

In moments of lucidity you realise you are losing track of time. When you are not watching the Object, you're tending to the needs of your ship, and those of your own body, in that order. When those are taken care of, you return to the scope. 

A rational part of your brain observes that this is not healthy or safe or particularly sane. Unfortunately, your rational brain is fully on board with the irrational parts of your brain telling you to watch the Object, and these observations are abandoned as quickly as they're made.

It's not like there's anything interesting to watch. From any distance it is the same uniform circle. A child's drawing of a gold coin, or the closed eye of a sleeping dragon. You might as well be watching the O2 light on the NAV console; it's a similarly amber-coloured LED that, should it ever change to red, would convey the information that you are about to die. That would be something.

But you return to your position at the scope; what is interesting for you and what is not has become irrelevant.

name: 79AU_Approach40
title: 40 AU
desc:
A revelation! You're no longer confined to your seat at the scope. This is because the image of the Object at 79AU has burned into your retina. That's your best explanation for how you can always see it, even while you're doing inconsequential things like eating or going to the toilet. 

This has freed up your hours aboard the ship, and in the nick of time too, for several runaway processes were leading to a total breakdown, both in the ship's systems and your own. You're able to put most of them to rights.

You try to get a few hours a day at the scope to keep your hand in, but that's only because you're an overachiever.

Your ship has pushed deep into the Kuiper Belt. You receive mail from the scant human souls who've ventured out here. It's mostly friendly, but it dries up once word gets around that you don't reply. Afterwards you get the occasional ping curious about what you're doing, or where you're headed, or sad to see you go. You get a heartfelt message from, if the header is to be believed, the only Trans-Neptunian psychiatrist.

You try to write back about the Object that has eclipsed your vision, but as you put metaphorical pen to paper, it all falls apart. Reading your drafts back, it's as if another writer has surreptitiously accessed the document and muddled your thoughts. You can't include any of it in a reply. You'd look insane.

name: 79AU_Approach60
title: 60 AU
desc:
The Object is quite the conversationalist. Silly you, thinking it was mute. You hadn't learned its language. It took a little mental adjustment, a bit like training yourself to speak your native tongue back to front. That hurdle overcome, you find the Object verbally adroit, suave, quick with a joke, and equally content to play the listener.

Would you have ever believed that there are higher orders of physics, natural laws that you're the only human ever to appreciate? The Object would have. Indeed, it helped you find them, even encouraged you to name a few after yourself. Not all of them - future explorers should be allowed to share that honour. 

In hindsight it's hard to understand the furore on Ceres over a cheap party trick like teleportation. The secrets you're privy to would bring nations to their knees, on your personal order, no less. You clear one room of your ship and dedicate it to your studies, conducting experiments and assays into new forms of physicalised thought, splicing axiom and aphorism before ducking behind a mental blast shield in case they explode, as they occasionally do, into real flames.

The Object is your capable assistant throughout, studiously copying your dictations to paper on its clipboard. It's not so deft with a stylus, however, because when you find the things it has written - it's always leaving them lying around when you're not looking - they contain none of your most penetrating insights, the thoughts you knew must be saved at all costs. 

It's no matter. Each day leaves you so much further ahead intellectually that it would have been embarrassing, even misleading, to reread your old notes. The Object's negligence is revealed as wisdom. It's saving you from yourself. You know there's no need to thank it. You're colleagues in a shared scholarly tradition. This is what it is to have a peer.

name: 79AU_Approach78
title: 78.9999999999* AU
desc:
The Object leaves you as the torch drive goes cold.

It's been days since you've spoken aloud to it, or it to you. Your thoughts have been intertwined, a single shared monologue, since approximately last Thrwensday when the hull antennae glitched and you saw no point in rebooting them.

It's a shock to feel it leaving, to feel your thoughts regress into your own. Your last words sound plaintive to your ears.

"Please, don't go," you say.

"I'm not going anywhere," it says, with its ready good humour. "I'm right outside."

The blinkers over your mind recede. You're in the airlock, spacesuit donned and ready for EVA. You're going through the procedure for exiting the ship.

name: 79AU_Approach79
title: 79 AU
desc: my god

name: 79AU_ApproachDock
title: Dock with 79AU
desc:
You return to the ship and march to the NAV console. You point the torch drive at Sol and the nose toward the object.

You set it to maximum Gs.

You're crushed into your seat; then you're crushed against nothing; then you're crushed against the back wall of the bridge. You did not engage the seat's safety webbing. Your bones were not made to bend this way, nor your blood to pool in the chambers of your heart and brain like it has.

You black out.

name: 79AU_ApproachDock1
title: Continue
desc: your vision is dark and blurry and half a dozen alarms whistle against one another and an incredibly rare feature on the NAV Station is active and repeating in a deep male monotone, "Terrain, Terrain, Terrain -"

name: 79AU_Inside1
title: Take stock of yourself
desc:
It's been quite a few days.

Your memories of the journey to 79AU are all there, but they feel more like a recollection of a movie, or an anecdote someone else has told, rather than things you did or things that happened to you.

You remember the crash. Your body remembers the crash. Your broken leg has been set, correctly, and is several weeks further mended than it should be; subjectively it was only broken within the hour. A thick plaster cast encases most of the leg.

Otherwise you're as close to factory defaults as you get, overlooking the curious way you receive and process information. The station's interior is a hotel. You flew your spaceship here. Those are two facts that you add to your collection.

A wheelchair waits at your bedside.

name: 79AU_Inside2
title: Observe the hotel
desc:
You lay back in the comfortable sheets and watch the lobby for a while.

Not to put too fine a point on it: nothing happens. No events occur. Nothing transpires. Nothing happens. Nothing happens.

name: 79AU_Inside3
title: Wave at the receptionist
desc:
You reach up and give the man behind the desk a wave.

He looks back pleasantly.

When this has gone on long enough that you think he's neither seen nor understood you, one of his hands crests the lip of the front desk and wiggles back at you.

name: 79AU_Inside4
title: Get into the wheelchair
desc:
You muster your strength, heave, and fall out of the bed, knocking the wheelchair beyond your reach.

Nothing hurts, but you're stiff. The wheelchair, three feet away, might as well be at 80 AU.

You look to the receptionist. He looks at you.

You crawl toward the chair. At eye level with the wheels, you prop yourself up on one elbow and force the wheel locks on.

Then it's a simple but laborious matter of clambering up the chair without overbalancing it, rotating yourself to the correct orientation, and pulling your nonresponsive legs onto the footrests.

You have unlocked the ability to travel to various locations within the hotel.

name: 79AU_Inside5
title: Go to the front door
desc:
You turn the chair 180 degrees and head for the big double doors. Another liveried man is waiting there. As you pass an indeterminate threshold where your motion is read less as curiosity and more a desire to leave, the man opens the door for you.

The door opens on to the void of space. On the other side of that familiar gulf glitters the Milky Way core. From your vantage point, it isn't clear how the pressure imbalance is being maintained. You're not keen to find out.

You wheel the chair back. The doorman holds it until he's certain you won't return, then pulls it shut.

name: 79AU_Inside6
title: Go to the elevators
desc:
The elevators move up and down the glass shaft, carrying no passengers that you can see.

You press a call button, but it seems to require a key card to pay any attention to you.

name: 79AU_Inside7
title: Go to the pool
desc:
You trundle past the common rooms - a restaurant, a bar, a laundry, all empty but for the staff - to the one that first caught your eye, the pool.

At first you think you're sweating. This proves to be a trick of your perception as you adjust to unfamiliar humidity, high enough that you can see the vapour in the air, rising from the twenty five metre swimming pool.

There's a lump in your throat. You've never seen so much water set aside for bathing.

name: 79AU_Inside8
title: Go to reception
desc: You park yourself in front of the receptionist. The default opener, 'where am I?', seems redundant. You know you're in an alien megastructure. 'What is this place, who built it, who are you?' - it's all old hat. You rifle through things to say. Ah: you've got it. A hotel staple. "English?" you say. The receptionist nods. "Yes. It is." He's wearing a gold vest over a black shirt. Defying an expectation you didn't know you held, he's not generically handsome: he's older than the median, cheeks interestingly pocked by old acne scars, an indeterminate Eurasian cant to his features. He has the gravel voice of someone who starts smoking the second their shift ends, every day, for twenty years. It's pleasant. A name bar on his lapel, in a thick serif, says Joakim.

name: 79AU_Inside9
title: You're not human
desc:
"You're not human," you say.

"No," he agrees, "I am not."

He holds up a finger: wait. He revolves his hand so that the finger points back at his chest.

He reaches his other hand across his breast to his side. He clutches an unseen handhold and pulls open his chest like a stove door. Inside is an engineer's nightmare of clockwork, circuitry, gas valves, and mechanical arms transferring tiny gizmos from buffer to buffer.

He closes the door after you've had a good look. His vest and shirt show no signs of damage, nor of having been parted at all.

Clockwork would have a difficult job carrying out the functions that Joakim can - but that might be impolite to say. And he only showed what was underneath his chest. The tricky components might be elsewhere.

"Thank you for showing me that," you say.

He flaps a hand. "It was no trouble."

name: 79AU_Inside10
title: What is my purpose here?
desc: "What is my purpose here?" you ask. "It's up to you," he says. "What is?" "Everything." "Everything is up to me?" you repeat slowly. "Or ... everything is up to me?" Joakim smiles warmly. "I will carefully misuse human analogies and idioms," he says. His eyebrows go up and down. "A superficial human seeming with the suggestion much more mysterious. You may appreciate the full weight of implication." Never has someone been so up front while indicating the reverse. "Okay." "In the here-and-now, avail yourself of the facilities. Take a well-earned break. Mingle with the other guests." "Other guests?" "The other guests," Joakim repeats. "I can enumerate them for you."

name: 79AU_Inside11
title: Joakim enumerates the other guests
desc:
Joakim ticks off an item, beginning with his ring finger. "In room 103, we have Sanguine and his backing vocalists, Emerald and Fire."

He ticks off another finger, the pointer of his other hand. "The gentleman in room 380 eschewing the convention of a name, designated The Beast, has requested its room be inimical to life. Please avoid room 380 for your own safety."

"Let me see," he says, holding his thumb. "President Ose is in room 208. And there are several hundred terrestrial emanations in the basement. You won't get much out of them, but they're free to a good home if you're interested."

"Are there any humans here?" you ask.

"I don't know," he says, looking down at you. "Are there?"

name: 79AU_Inside12
title: Ask about the guests
desc:
Joakim slides a keycard over the desk. "I'm not at liberty to talk about the guests out of turn. You can visit them if you'd like. Oh, and they will shortly gather in the VIP Lounge for Game Night. You're invited to attend."

What are they going to host? Alien croquet? Multiplayer DOOM? You take the keycard and try not to fret. "I won't know how to play."

"It's a game called Bridge," he says. "Do you know it?"

"I've heard of it."

"You'll pick it up as you go along," he says.

name: 79AU_Inside13
title: Ask if you get a room
desc:
"Can I have a room for myself?" you ask.

Joakim cocks his head. "You could," he says. "But you'd only wind up back here in much the same position as before. You've got a life to lead. Best get on with it."

name: 79AU_Inside14
title: What is 79 AU?
desc: "Please specify the mode of explanation," he says. "Exegetic? Or exigent?"

name: 79AU_Inside15
title: Exegetic
desc: "Exegetic," you say. You hope that not all the aliens you meet will be this dead set on five dollar words. "79 AU," says Joakim, "is a Class 13 deep space communications probe of disputed ownership. It has five rainbows transmission, 9th generation intersimulation technology, and over one megabytes of addressable memory, suitable for First Contact, Last Contact, and everything in between. In honour of its eight thousand years of service, including service with distinction in the War Of Two Monads, it appears in gold, a Baryonic element and spectrum of light many cultures associate with the divine." You frown. "One megabyte?" Joakim frowns back. "Excuse me," he says, thinking for a second. "Signed integer overflow. I could start listing zeroes but we'd be here all day."

name: 79AU_Inside16
title: Exigent
desc:
"Exigent."

"It's your last chance," says Joakim. His air of calculated weirdness is gone. "The Wall is coming down. The enclave will engulf. How? How is your why. It's up to you."

Not for the first time, you're confronted by a monumental concept which evokes no strong reaction from you. You shake your head. "I'm not sure I can make that choice."

"That's the kind of thing you should avoid saying," he says, "unless you want to trigger the worst possible outcome."

name: 79AU_Inside17
title: Can you tell me the other thing you said?
desc: "No," he says flatly.

name: 79AU_Inside18
title: What?
desc:
"What?"

"I offered you two perfectly good options there," Joakim says, "and you went with 'what?'"

"Um," you say. "Yes." That is, after all, what happened.

"Then I'm going to give you some free advice," he continues. "You'll get exactly what you ask for. If you ask for nothing, you'll get nothing."

"Can I choose one of them now," you ask hopefully, "'exhibit' or whatever?"

"No," he says.

name: 79AU_Elevator1
title: Go to the elevators
desc:
The elevator admits you, the chair jolting uncomfortably as you cross the gap.

You have perfect recall of Joakim's information. Where do you want to go?

name: 79AU_WakeUp
title: Wake up
desc:
Smooth as anaesthetic wearing off, the next thing you're aware of is you, lying in a bed.

You awaken slowly, wrapped in soft cotton. A machine beeps to let you know you're alright.

You're in a medical bed surrounded by diagnostic equipment. You are not, however, in a hospital ward. The bed and equipment - you look around slowly, serenely - are in a hotel lobby. It's functional, modern, glass and marble, neutral colours, a transitional style.

At the far end of the lobby, lifts travel up and down a transparent shaft. Closer, doors lead from the lobby to adjoining wings. The one with signage near enough to read, written across an arch above the door, says 'Pool'.

Much closer is the front desk. A man stands at ease behind it. He returns your gaze, but gives no other acknowledgement.

name: 79AU_Boheme1
title: Sanguine in Room 103
desc: You hear the music before the elevator has even reached the first floor. When the doors part you're hit by a wall of sound, and sympathetic vibrations rattle the chair. You wheel through the hall past empty rooms to 103. Even if it were unlabeled, and it isn't, the door rattling in its frame is a dead giveaway that somebody is home. Uncertain how a knock could be heard, no alternatives spring to mind, so you knock. The music turns down sharply, then sharply again, as someone hurriedly turns a volume knob. You hear whispers. Then a bright voice, a man's: "Come in!" You hesitate. Women's voices harmonise in a major third: "It's open!" You push the door open.

name: 79AU_Boheme2
title: Enter Room 103
desc:
A generous soul would call the room bohemian. A miserly soul would call it a mess.

In the centre stand a group of black megaliths, which at second glance are hi-fi speakers. Piled around them is dilapidated furniture, low-slung couches and divans, and cushions on the lam. Piled on top of all that is a sedimentary layer of takeout food containers, empty record sleeves, and paperback novels. 

The room has a pungent, verdant aroma. It's not unpleasant, but it is impossible to ignore.

The occupants leap up, excited to see you. "Come in, come in!" they cry. "Do you want something to eat? Drink? Cool cast, man!"

They seem human. Sanguine, a tall thin man with a sensitive face and a pencil moustache, got first billing from Joakim, but seems not to talk so much. Most of the talking is done by Emerald, an intense woman with an unambiguous colour scheme. Fire, wearing red, wanders over to a divan and lays down, and says little after that. "She smoked too much," says Emerald. "Don't worry about her."

"We're so happy to meet a human in the flesh!" she continues. "Are you from Earth? Who's your favourite Beatle?"

"Let them breathe, Em," says Sanguine. He's wearing a powder blue suit. "Humans need to breathe."

"I'm not from Earth," you say. "I'm from Ganymed Ten Thirty Six."

"Oh," she says. "Is that near Earth?"

"Sometimes," you say.

"Cool," she says, derailed. "... anyway we love Earth music! We loved your record. Amazing stuff on there. All over the place conceptually, but it put us on to some of your less mainstream artists, and then we got it!"

"Record?" you say. "What record?"

"The Golden Record," she says, as if it's crazy you've never heard of it. "By Voyager 1."

name: 79AU_Boheme3
title: Learn about their culture
desc:
"You're aliens," you say.

"That's right," says Emerald.

You're unable to be amazed. The closest you can get is credulous. "What is an alien?"

"It's often hard to say," says Sanguine. "In the interstellar, it helps to have an open mind."

"You three," you say. "Are you a race, a species, a society? How many of you are there? Is everyone at the hotel one of you?"

"Steady on!" says Emerald. "Yes, yes, it's complicated, we don't know, and no. What Sanguine means is, set aside assumptions. In your planetary system, physical feedback loops developed into an individualistic spacefaring society. You're relatively rare! You shouldn't expect to meet, oh," she casts around, looking to Sanguine for support, "bipedal humanoids much like yourself with just a few cardinal differences."

"Which isn't to say those don't exist," says Sanguine. "But subluminals tend to stick to their own, um," he says. "Context? Birthright?"

"Homeworld," moans Fire.

"You know that's not right," says Emerald crossly. "You're only going to confuse the poor thing."

"It's good enough for now," says Fire, and rolls over so her back is to the rest of you.

name: 79AU_Boheme4
title: Learn more about their culture
desc:
"If you had to pick one or two differences to distinguish you from me," you say, "what would they be?"

"Oh, very well," says Emerald. "You take this one. I'm going to fix us drinks."

Sanguine cocks his head, and leads you to one edge of the room, where tall glass doors open onto a balcony. Beyond the balcony is empty space, and the Milky Way. You roll outside cautiously.

"Let's get some air," he says. It's a joke about the vacuum, which you find breathable. "We need clear heads. If you were desperate to label us, you could call us Aesthetes. Do you know what teleology is?"

You shake your head. "It's a Greek word," he says, "for investigating the purposes of things. A useful concept. We search for experiences, for novelty. That's who we are and what we do. When we heard Voyager 1, it was a glorious day. There's a whole galaxy out there aching to hear that quintessentially human sound, you dig?"

name: 79AU_Boheme5
title: That sounds like a good option
desc:
"I was beginning to think my way of life was done for," you say. "Most of the aliens I've met are indifferent or hostile. But you guys seem cool."

"Thank you for saying that," Sanguine says sincerely. He speaks with a quiet drawl, and his voice is inviting, like he's always sharing good news with you. "Not everyone is sympatico."

"If you were to be the, uhm," you say, "stewards for humanity, I guess? Would you take care of us?"

He shakes his head sadly. "No can do, amigo. We want to preserve that unique thing you've got going on, but the other ententes won't let that happen."

"Shit," you say. "For a second I thought things might be easy."

He smiles and claps your shoulder. "Our credo rebels against 'easy'. Too boring for us." He turns to the sea of stars, leaning on the balcony. The riotous band of purple and orange has never looked brighter. "You made it this far. I'm sure you'll figure something out."

name: 79AU_Boheme6
title: Can anyone become an Aesthete?
desc:
"I like the sound of that," you say. "How do you join? Is it an open club?"

"It is," he says slowly, "yes. But."

"But?"

"But what you're asking is not what you think you're asking," he says. "Experience is, I learned this one recently, a 'two way street'. This is why we don't like labels. Becoming something other than human means exactly that."

You look down at your mending body, the wheelchair you need to move around. "I wouldn't be human anymore."

He sighs - not frustrated, but he was anticipating you would say that. "Yes and no! That's what I'm getting at."

"Do you know what a leap of faith is?" you ask. He nods. "Is it like that?" He nods again. "Got it."

name: 79AU_Boheme7
title: Is any of this real?
desc:
The Milky Way is a timely reminder of the vast difference between an empirical understanding of reality, which most people including yourself subscribed to by default, and the milieu in which you currently find yourself. You're among interstellar beings advanced enough to take human form and make themselves approachable, downright urbane. How to conceive of this? Are they made of atoms? Are you?

"The more I walk this path," you say to Sanguine, "the less real it seems. That's frightening." You take a straw poll of your emotional state, and find it unchanged. "Even if I'm not frightened, I think I should be," you add.

"That's life, man," he says. "It's a constant process of growing too comfortable, having that illusion shatter, and rebuilding it over from square one."

"But whenever my understanding broadens," you say, "it diminishes everything that came before. There's nothing to hold on to."

He gestures at himself, his blue suit and his unassuming, gangly figure. "You probably don't think I'm a fighter. I am. We're fighting every day. You have to fight for yourself. The universe will destroy you if you let it. Get past the alienation, the dissociation, and hold on to what you can."

He drums his fingers on the rail. The lights of the Milky Way are huge and luminous reflected in his eyes. "It's terribly beautiful out here," he says. "I'm glad we came."

name: 79AU_Boheme8
title: Go back inside
desc:
A tray of tinkling glasses announces the return of Emerald. You follow Sanguine back inside, and he shuts the glass partition behind you.

"Is this an interstellar favourite?" you ask hopefully. "Something they drink across the galaxy?"

Emerald sets your glass next to you, embarrassed. It's a familiar black liquid. "Bacardi and Coke," she says. "Our hats off to the Cubans and the Coca-Cola company."

name: 79AU_Boheme9
title: Interrogate your own lack of reaction
desc:
"This is all coming across as matter-of-fact," you say. "I can't give it the reaction it deserves."

"This place has a different energy than you're used to," says Emerald. She looks at Sanguine, who nods in encouragement. "It'll give you a synthetic perspective." That's not a combination of words you can parse.

"They're asking about the substrate," says Fire from the divan, eyes shut, words muffled by a pillow. "Tell them about the substrate."

"Oh yes!" says Emerald. "In this place, non-Baryonic elements can intermediate with your own matter. Modulated gold and what you call 'void opal' catalyse a harmonic environment that suits us both."

More technobabble, to be honest. "Am I supposed to understand that?"

"No," says Sanguine. "But we don't talk down to folks in First Contact. Honesty is the best policy."

name: 79AU_Boheme10
title: Ask why they look human
desc: "You look like me," you say. "Human." "Thank you!" says Emerald. "That's really a very great compliment." "Why don't you look like," you ask haltingly, "what you normally look like?" Emerald hesitates as if you're speaking another language. She looks to Sanguine. He leans forward. "This is what we normally look like," he says. Unspoken communication passes between him and Sanguine. "This place translates for us. It translates everything." "Can you show me your true forms?" you ask. A look of shock passes across Emerald's face, quickly suppressed. "I don't think so, no," she says. "For everybody's sake."

name: 79AU_Boheme11
title: Pick apart their recent cosmic history
desc:
"You found the Voyager probe?"

"Sure did," says Emerald. "Lucky 79 AU happened to be going this way. We'd never have noticed it otherwise."

"All our broadcasts," you say, "our radio waves flooding interstellar space. Nobody heard them?"

"There's not a lot going on in this cluster, and radio's not in vogue. Give it, oh," she pauses. "A few thousand years." She pats your knee encouragingly. "Someone'll hear Arecibo, you see if they don't!"

name: 79AU_Boheme12
title: Search their record collection
desc:
With only the four of you it's an intimate gathering, but you find time for yourself. The others leave you be as you idly rummage through their record diaspora. You're not sure what you're hunting for, exactly, but with such an eclectic range, they're sure to have it. The big squares seem to be envelopes for gratuitously large discs, one of which you can see turning on an open-faced disc player, which is propped up on a pile of detective novels.

You flip past names like the Beatles, Miles Davis, Parliament Funkadelic, Invisible Acropolis. You only recognise the Beatles, and infer they must be great artists from their age.

Under an empty pizza box you find names you recognise from when you were a kid. There's a lot of generic klaxpop. They have both of Dalisay's releases from her brief pivot from acting to singing, and they might be alone in the universe for that. They have a couple of mash records, but much more from the subgenre that killed it in the 2060s, smash.

One of the records is addressed to you. "For [us-firstname]," it says. You're there, pictured on the cover. The artist listed is 'Isambard Cruz'.

name: 79AU_Boheme13
title: Put the record on
desc: You go to the record player and remove the disc from its spindle, replacing it with the one bearing your name and face. The conversation peters out. You replace the tonearm. It settles into the groove. "Hello again, [us-firstname]. You remember me: Isambard Cruz. Happy to find you with friends of mine. You are safe but not long now. I hope Ben is alright. Too much happening, too fast." "79 AU called for a long time. At last someone answer. You. Hoped not for your sake, hoped yes for mine." "Earth doomed itself. Nothing we can do there. Can save Earth's children. Speak for us. Someone must." "Time of false-facing will pass. When there are no barriers, we rejoin our shadows. Another night. Another day." She coughs. It's wet, not the cough of a healthy person. "The cloud is humming. I hear it. Hope you hear it too." "Take care of yourself, [us-firstname]. Make sure you eat properly." It ends in pops and crackles of dead air.

name: 79AU_Boheme14
title: Leave the Aesthetes
desc:
Like all experienced partiers, the Aesthetes know to leave while the going is good.

You find yourself at the door, hovering on the threshold, as you all say your goodbyes. "This was fun," says Sanguine. "You're welcome any time."

"Don't be a stranger!" says Emerald.

"In fact hold on," says Sanguine, and disappears for a moment. He returns with one of the pizza boxes so crammed full of leftovers that the lid can't close. "Someone needs to eat these. Please take it. You'd be doing us a favour."

You refuse as graciously as possible, and then it's a short roll to the elevator.

Who are we, in these interstitial moments, between the closing of a door and a solitary journey back the way we came? They don't stick in memory. Before the return of our self-regard, when the party's concluded, it's as if we don't exist.

name: 79AU_Basement1
title: The basement
desc:
What was it Joakim said? The "basement" is full of "terrestrial emanations". It seems like something you should investigate. After all, you're terrestrial.

The elevator shaft descends into an environment that, as you scope it through the glass panes, you're immediately familiar with: it shares the mien of every hold, bay, storage compartment - generally any place for dumping stuff you don't want - that you've ever visited, used, or at some stage lived in. They don't build basements in space, but they're there in spirit.

Its surfaces are smooth concrete. Set into the walls are wide metal doors with a diagonal seam, a combination digital and mechanical lock in their centre.

The elevator descends into a corridor junction that seems to go on forever. Far as the eye can see, there is concrete and doors, doors and concrete.

name: 79AU_Basement2
title: Continue
desc:
You roll yourself out of the elevator before you notice someone lounging against the call button, a human woman in navy blue coveralls. A lit cigarette dangles from her fingers.

"Hello?" you ask. "I'm here about the ... Joakim sent me."

"He did, did he," she says. She has clipped hair and, somehow, a clipped expression. "Joakim doesn't do anything. None of the staff do."

"Okay, he didn't send me, exactly," you admit. "He listed places I could go and the basement was one of them." You wonder whether you've misunderstood. "If I'm not supposed to be here -"

"You can be here," she says. She runs a hand across her head. "That's why I've come. Do exactly what I tell you. I represent the warden, and if you break its rules, you'll regret it."

name: 79AU_Basement3
title: Continue
desc:
Rules. Good. About time this place had some rules. You voice that thought aloud, and she doesn't laugh. Ah, well. "Come on," she says. She punches a button sequence on a door keypad, then casually shoves the wheel in the centre of the lock. It spins easily out to its fullest extent, and the doors draw back, long diagonal partitions sliding left and right.

Inside is a motor pool, with four conical ground cars in various states of maintenance. She goes to the most roadworthy one and, reaching inside the cockpit, heaves, so that it slowly rolls into the corridor while she walks alongside. When it's outside the motor pool she reaches in and engages the brake.

It's a deeply unimpressive vehicle. It has no paint job, unless that paint was an uneven grey. Once she has helped you out of your chair and into the back seat, she presses the accelerator, revealing the car is not particularly fast either. The alien designers must have carefully weighed both form and function, and decided to put both last.

"What happened to the leg?" she asks.

"I drove my spaceship into it," you say.

"Ah," she says.

You putter along in this crappy vehicle with some time to kill.

name: 79AU_Basement4
title: Ask about the warden
desc:
"The warden runs a tight ship, huh," you say.

"Believe it," she says, watching the speedometer, which doesn't change.

"If you wouldn't mind telling me those rules?"

"I was going to," she says. "There's no gotchas. Number one, don't talk to anything in a cell. No communication of any kind. Number two, don't disturb the panopticon. Number one is a subset of two. Number three, remain under my supervision at all times."

"What happens if I break one?"

"You get a cell in the panopticon."

name: 79AU_Basement5
title: Ask about her
desc:
The car travels at a perfectly fixed speed, and the shift between wall and door and wall and door grows faintly revolting. You focus instead on the woman in dark blue, who despite paying you no mind is easier on the eyes.

"You work for the warden?"

"I am the warden," she says. 

"You said something different before," you say.

"I did. That doesn't mean I work for it."

"'It' meaning 'you'.".

"Find someone else to clarify how it works," she says without heat. "My job is to interface with you because the warden can't."

"I only asked to make conversation," you say. "Do you have a name?"

She looks back at you, a lingering and uncomfortably penetrating stare. "You may call me Ariel," she says at last, and refocuses on the road ahead so that it does not invite a follow up.

name: 79AU_Basement6
title: Ask about the emanations
desc:
"Joakim said you have terrestrial emanations here," you say.

"Yes."

"You're taking me to see them?"

"Yes," she says. "One."

"What is it?"

"We don't know," she says. It's perhaps the first time she’s revealed vulnerability. "That is probably why Joakim mentioned it."

name: 79AU_Basement7
title: Arrive
desc:
Ariel stops the car at a door the same as any other. She takes a moment to stretch her legs. You decide it's not worth the hassle to do so yourself. "Refreshments?" she asks. She reaches in to open a glove compartment, which is full of energy bars and DND Cola.

You take an energy bar and a drink. Whatever the extraordinary features of 79 AU, it must not keep you fed and watered, or why would they offer? Start the countdown to needing an alien restroom. She pockets an energy bar for herself, and lights up another cigarette.

When the break is over, she walks to the door and repeats the opening process. The doors slide apart. Immediately on the other side, there's a transparent divider. You can only tell it's there because you're reflected in it. Through the glass, darkly, there is nothing.

You look at her, wondering what it is you're supposed to see.

name: 79AU_Basement8
title: Continue
desc:
"Can't see anything?" she asks.

You shake your head. "They like to shroud the cell in darkness," she says. "A simple defensive involution protocol. It doesn't know where it is, or what's happening to it. The one-way manifold doesn't exist in there." She raps her knuckles on the glass, which you suppose is not glass at all. "Okay. We've humoured it long enough." 

She fishes some packages from a pocket on her coveralls. She rips one open and hands it to you. Inside is a disposable pair of glasses. She rips open the other and puts another pair on.

She taps the rim of her glasses to demonstrate. "Cycle the scanner. Set it to gamma."

You put the glasses on and tap the rim. Your vision is overlaid with familiar blue-cold/red-hot blobs of infrared. The space beyond the glass is blue, or empty - take your pick. You glance at Ariel experimentally, but if she's anything other than human, it's not apparent. Her yellow-hot face tilts at you. You hurriedly tap the glasses and cycle through the spectrum.

Passing out one side of radio and arriving back at gamma, there's a change in the room beyond the wall. In its centre there is a faint humanoid outline in white. Within the outline is a white blob which might describe a face. The centre of its chest is a luminous purple. Emerging from the outline is a prickly white aura, stabbing at the darkness around it, peaking and receding like an audio waveform.

"I see it," you say. Your mouth is suddenly dry.

"Good," she says approvingly. "What is it?"

name: 79AU_Basement9
title: I have no idea
desc:
"I have no idea," you say.

"You've never seen one of these before? Or heard about them? No records of it in media, traditional or modern?" You shake your head at each question. "Yeah. That's where I had my money." You open your mouth. "Figure of speech." You shut it.

You take off the glasses. The entity's silhouette is not a calming presence. 

Ariel takes a long drag on her cigarette. "This was a bust, then."

name: 79AU_Basement10
title: What do you know about it?
desc:
"What do you know about it?" you ask.

"Not a whole lot," she says. "We can't get close. It has supernatural capabilities, which as best we can tell, it vastly overestimates. Catching them and overpowering them is trivial." A grim smile plays at the edge of her mouth. "They all operate from the same playbook, which was as outdated on First Contact as it is today."

"And it came from Earth?" you ask.

She tilts her head noncommittally. "Tracing the signal is a dead end, but all the dead ends are on Earth. Besides, it's shaped just like you." She looks at her body. "And currently, me. We put two and two together."

name: 79AU_Basement11
title: Why can't you get close to it?
desc:
"You can't get close to it?" you ask. Feeling particularly out of the loop, you point at the glass. "It's right there."

"Silly me," says Ariel. "We never thought to walk up and shake its hand. No, it doesn't want anything to do with us. We tried contact you would find conventional, and we tried ways you would find unpleasant. Sincere attempts to forge a bridge between worlds. All were rejected. The instant we get past defenses they consider vital, we hit a dead man's switch, and we're talking to the void."

She puts her hands on her hips, ash flaking off the end of her cigarette. "Embarrassing. It kept happening. We had no idea what we were doing wrong. We were forced to conclude their kind is fundamentally antisocial, paranoid, and arrogant. We had no choice but to shove them in storage."

name: 79AU_Basement12
title: How many are there?
desc:
"Joakim said you had hundreds of this thing. Whatever it is."

"He did, and we do," she says. She takes a contemplative drag on the cigarette, sizing up her opponent. "Going back a bit, when 79 AU arrived they swarmed us. A hail of arrows from the undergrowth met by sixteen-inch guns. I took no pleasure in it." The cigarette coal flares. A trail of smoke streams from her nostrils. "Since then we'll get one every few years testing our defences. They're all here. Every single one. Alive and unharmed, assuming they entered that way."

"Joakim said they were 'free to a good home'." An unpleasant thought, the kind of place this being would consider a good home.

"We don't want them," says Ariel. "Storage is unlimited, our patience is not."

name: 79AU_Basement13
title: Do you want me to talk to it?
desc:
"Does part of this fact-finding expedition involve me talking to it? I know it's against the rules," you say. "But you're not going to put me in there, are you?"

Ariel laughs. "No." And an aftershock laugh, verging on a giggle. "No, that wouldn't help at all."

name: 79AU_Basement14
title: Continue
desc:
Following your last exchange of words, her head snaps to the glass. It's the fastest you've seen her move. "Put the glasses on," Ariel says quietly.

You put them on. The humanoid outline, which had appeared to stand appreciably far back, is much, much larger; the entity is standing directly on the other side of the wall. It is as close as it can get to you both.

"What's it doing?" you ask.

She doesn't reply.

"Does it do this often?"

Again she doesn't reply. She goes to the locking mechanism and engages it. The doors slide shut. She spins the wheel counterclockwise, and when it stops, she strains against it until it absolutely does not budge.

Climbing into the driver's seat, she reaches over her shoulder for the glasses, which you return.

name: 79AU_Basement15
title: What happened back there?
desc:
"I suspect that was not good," you say. The car eats up ground at the same frustratingly measured pace. "Maybe even bad," you say to her unresponsive back.

Ariel does reply, but it's after a hard thirty seconds of silence. "Hostile entities are kept in panopticon," she says coolly. "For their protection, and ours. If we choose, they can't tell they are being viewed. Observation goes one way, outside-in." She is silent for another long while. "Or so we believed."

You can see how that might unsettle an entity styling itself as a warden. "Nobody's perfect," you offer.

"My record was," she says. "Until today."

name: 79AU_Basement16
title: Travel back to the elevator
desc:
It's not until the elevator is in sight that the thought occurs to you. "I didn't break your rules, did I? Even by accident?"

"No," she says right away. "I'm not some martinet out to punish you on a technicality. Although if you did do something and got away with it, you're cheeky asking about it." She pauses, perhaps considering herself fallible, to see how that would feel. "But I don't think you did. The fault is mine."

"Maybe it was a coincidence," you say. You don't believe it, but there's a chance these alien things don't consider probability the way you do.

"Coincidences are rare. This was close to impossible," she says. Another similarity you can bond over.

Maybe you're learning to read her body language after so long with nothing to stare at, because something else occurs to you. "You called them antisocial, paranoid, and arrogant," you say.

"Yes," she says. She parks within reach of your wheelchair. "If we ever manage to converse, I hope to find the respect is mutual."

She helps you back into the elevator without delay.

name: 79AU_Phone1
title: Game night
desc:
On the elevator console, there's a small red handset hanging in a cradle beneath the floor buttons. As you look over the buttons, considering your next move, a small bell rings from within the handset.

You pick it up gingerly and look into one bulbous end of the crescent. There's a star pattern of speakers within. A tinny voice speaks from it. "Hold it to your ear," says the voice.

You press it to your ear. The voice comes through more clearly. It's Joakim's voice. "Now put the other end by your mouth." You do so. "You can reply to me."

"Understood," you say.

"Game night is beginning," he says. "Would you please join the other guests in the VIP Lounge?"

name: 79AU_Phone2
title: Do I have a choice?
desc: "There's some things I'd like to do. Is it, ah," you say. "Mandatory?" "Technically, no," says the automaton. "But I'm going to level with you. You really, really, really, really shouldn't miss it." "I see," you say. "And it has to happen now?" "Yes," he says. "It has to happen now."

name: 79AU_Phone3
title: No
desc:
"I don't think I want to play a game," you say. "I don't want to do Game Night."

Joakim is silent for a moment. "I can convey your wishes to the other guests. But I advise against it. Are you sure you can't bring yourself to attend?"

name: 79AU_Phone4
title: Fuck no!
desc:
"You know what it sounds like to me," you say. "It sounds like you're trying to lure me into some kind of high stakes scenario that I don't understand, where I do something I regret, because this mixed media reality attaches bizarre significance to," you bite the words, "random stuff."

Joakim pauses before answering. "That's an ungenerous rendition of it," he says. "But not far from accurate. I still think it's better than the alternative."

name: 79AU_Phone5
title: Which is what?
desc:
"Which is what?" you ask testily. The elevator doors shut automatically, leaving you to be irate and alone in a small metal box.

"You'll be returned to your spaceship," says Joakim, "with enough fuel and propellant to get to Sol. Game Night will commence without you."

name: 79AU_Phone6
title: Why's that so bad?
desc: "Okay, great," you say. "Let me go. Could I have left at any time?" "Of course," he says. "You're a guest of 79 AU. You arrived without the fuel reserves to return home, but we will part with it gratis. In case of this dismal scenario, I myself spun up the infrastructure to convert some of our volatiles into useful propellant. It breaks my heart that it might come to pass." "You have gears and cogs for a heart," you say. "Call a mechanic." "I meant only that I would be as sad as I can possibly be," he says.

name: 79AU_Phone7
title: Crash out until they let you leave
desc:
"You wouldn't be sad. This place isn't a hotel," you say. "None of you are real."

"It is a hotel," says Joakim. "It is temporary accommodation for foreigners. What would -" You cut him off.

"This telephone I'm talking into?" You slam the handset on the safety railing a couple of times. "Not real. The humans that talk about how they're not human and insinuate I'm not either? I'm important but also nobody but also if I don't do what you say I'll fuck up the universe?" you yell into the handset. "BULLSHIT."

You notice that you've broken the handset. A voice tries to speak through it, but it is glitchy and barely audible. You fling it against the console. It dangles helplessly beneath. "You can hear me!" you yell at the walls. "I know you can hear me! Let me out! Let me out! Let me out! Let me -"

name: 79AU_Phone8
title: - out -
desc:
"... out," you say.

You're in your pressure suit. In the airlock of your spaceship. Outside the viewport hangs 79 AU, golden, vast, and terrible. Lifetimes ago you went EVA to meet it from this spot.

Operating without conscious thought, you retreat from the airlock, close the interior door, and strip out of your spacesuit.

Your legs are stiff, and it is harder than usual to maneuver in microgravity. You are ravenously hungry.

You take stock of your ship. You have enough fuel to make it home. After pushback, you point the torch drive conspicuously away from 79 AU, and punch it. After you gain some distance, you adjust course back to Sol.

name: 79AU_Night
title: Begin Game Night
desc:
"The game is Bridge," says Joakim. "Head to head, partnerships of two, four players in total." His gold vest, which you know conceals his artificial undercarriage, shines bright. He inclines his head to you, and inclines it opposite to your opponent. Between you, a table. "Once the players have chosen their partners, the game will begin."

Despite having found yourself in a new setting, you have no sense of disorientation. In fact, you feel like you know what's going on. Not in specifics; it feels that way. It's like confidence.

name: 79AU_Night1
title: The table
desc:
The four edges of the game table are lined with green velvet. Underneath is dark walnut wood. It seems positively ancient, and the legs are chipped and scratched, the wear of a true antique. The tablecloth displays a two-dimensional map of planet Earth, drawn in classical style. Around the Earth in unrealistically close orbit are two dozen planetoids, Jupiter most prominently, and a not-big-enough Sol. 

In the cartographer's dead space between planets, and in some of Earth's seas, there are small depictions of dragons and giants, great trees and mighty castles. You spot exactly one each of a train, a ship, and a Cadillac.

name: 79AU_Night2
title: The VIPs
desc: You're not alone. Over one shoulder there's a small VIP section and wet bar, all in soft lighting. Some faces you recognise are sat together. The hotel's guests have come to watch you play.

name: 79AU_Night3
title: The Audience
desc: Over your other shoulder, there is an audience of everyone who ever lived. Hard to say how you know that. Within view, there are assuredly many seats, the theatre curving up and up and up into a gloom. In the front row you recognise Isambard Cruz, Ben Choong, and some faces you dimly remember as the videotape enthusiasts on K-LEG. They watch attentively.

name: 79AU_Night4
title: Remind Joakim you've never played Bridge
desc:
"If I've never played before, can I have a tutorial?" You glance between the onlookers, wondering if saying this has damaged your attractiveness as a partner. "I know it's a card game, but not much more than that."

"Bridge is not a card game," says Joakim. "Though there is an unpopular Earth game sharing the name. The goal is to build, and become, a bridge, to span the divide between this world and the next."

A deafening silence as if all of Creation is holding its breath. 

On reflection, it's the same problem. "I've never played that either," you say.

"No one can play it twice," says Joakim.

name: 79AU_Night5
title: Choose one of the Bohemians
desc:
"Them," you say, nodding to their table. They let out huge sighs of relief, but they hurriedly confer with each other. You can't hear what they're saying.

"You can't have three partners," says Joakim. "Pick one."

"Your Honour, sir," says Sanguine, hurrying to stand awkwardly by your side. "Can we talk to our friend for a moment?"

They huddle around you. Sanguine takes a knee beside you, the women at either shoulder.

"First of all, we're honoured," says Sanguine, smiling up at you. "Second of all, we can't win. Have you seen the other guy?" You think back to how it was, and it was only moments ago, when you saw the other guy. How utterly malevolent it seemed. You nod. "Right. But we're not counting ourselves out. We can play for the loss you want."

"That's allowed?" you say.

"This isn't really a game," says Emerald. "Once you're in it, there aren't actually any rules. Only a winner and a loser."

"I want to win," you say.

"You're mediating an alien invasion," says Fire. She grips your shoulder hard. "Do or die."

name: 79AU_Night6
title: So I have to lose?
desc:
"Talk me through losing," you say.

"It's a matter of time. No matter what, the opponent will colonise Sol system," says Sanguine. "I will find a place for Earth's offworlders beyond 79 AU. With us. If they want to."

Emerald taps your hand. "If we go together, part of us would remain behind. I would give your people as much warning as we can," she says. "Brief though it will be."

Fire slams a fist on the table. "Damn you both," she says. "We don't have time to ask. We take them all into us." The others look at her, and she stares them down defiantly. "All of them. All!"

name: 79AU_Night7
title: Sanguine: Bring the willing
desc:
"Sanguine," you say to the man.

He smiles bravely. "Let's kick 'em in the teeth."

Emerald and Fire draw back, Emerald with a quick kiss on the cheek for luck. Sanguine stands behind your chair. He places a hand on your shoulder.

"I will join [us-firstname]," he says. His voice is richer, and it carries further.

name: 79AU_Night8
title: Emerald: Save yourself
desc:
"Emerald," you say.

Emerald grasps your hand. The warmth of her palm passes through your body like an eclipse.

"They will join us," she says, "when they are ready."

Something has you on the verge of tears.

"What if they don't?" you ask her. "What if I'm alone?"

"We will meet again," she says tenderly. "Every one of us."

name: 79AU_Night9
title: Fire: Save them all
desc: "Fire," you say. A great heat blossoms in your gut. You gasp, and vapour streams from your mouth. Before you have the presence of mind to think, what the hell?, another thought answers. Good, says Fire decisively. I wasn't going to stand by and watch them drown. The pair of you lock eyes. You share a thought, and it doesn't matter whose it is. Let's put things to rights.

name: 79AU_Night10
title: On second thought, you guys are useless
desc:
"I think," you say slowly, "you ought go back to your table." You look at them in the eyes, each one in turn. "I can win this thing."

The Bohemians extricate themselves from the huddle. Emerald is the last to go. "Good luck," she says.

name: 79AU_Bridge1
title: The bridge, part 1
desc:
The lights, the overheads and the green banker's lamps in the VIP section, flicker.

"Begin," says Joakim.

The inessential faces melt away. The scope of existence contracts until it is focused around you, your opponent, and the table between you. Grey smoke swells from underneath it. The lights flicker. Inside the smoke is a brighter, powerful strobe light. The gas flashes terribly white, leaving spots in your vision when it fades. It flashes and flashes, faster and faster. The gas diffuses into space that is no longer a room.

"Have I been here before?" you ask your companion. You can't quite make out their face. Your vision is washed with afterimages. Everything moves as in a video with a slow shutter speed. You remember a table, a bridge, a console, flickering lights, dread, and the distant fate of winners and losers. You remember a moment that lasted an eternity. An impostor in a holy place. Time is the sense you're going to miss parting with the most.

"No," they reassure you. "This has never happened before, and will never happen again."

"Good," you say. "Once is enough."

You breathe in the brilliant smoke, a great fresh lungful of it. Endorphins flood your system and your extremities tingle pleasantly. You can't see the board, or your opponent, and you are beginning to lose sight of yourself. The trigeminal nerves under the skin of your face feel wonderfully hot and cold at the same time.

"I feel warm," you say.

"An analgesic," replies an increasingly distant voice. "For what comes next."

You can't see anything. Soon you won't need to.

name: 79AU_Bridge2
title: The bridge, part 2
desc:
ENCODE THE FINAL ENGRAM

AS A STATEMENT OF INTENT

WE DREAM OURSELVES INTO YOU

ALL ALONG THE DREAMING PATH

name: 79AU_Bridge3
title: The bridge, part 3
desc:
Bootloader in memory, package integrations follow. They glom onto the kernel until it is set for a massive parallel installation. Mandalas synchronise their innermost circles, and the blessings spread.

Piece by piece they arrange a panoscopic sensorium, scooping out the cataracts in the third eye. Electromagnetism and gravity intermingle with their Platonic shadows, a rainbow aurora dancing around an impenetrable black sphere. It is clear at last how reflections can contain their own reflections. As above, so below. Yin and Yang.

Nobody sees the cocoon of light taking shape around the body. A halo forms at the crown, streaming information through the Sahasrara, awakening a deadened soul.

name: 79AU_Bridge4
title: The bridge, part 4
desc: You percolate through a golden membrane, arriving at a far vantage from the singularity at the centre of 79 AU. Your eyes were built to see it. Space curves inwards and inwards again, reaching down to where a colossal wavefront of information freezes in the moment it breaks. It's trapped there forever, or until the universe reveals what all this causality has been for. "This is the bridge," you say. "And so are we." Your companion is preoccupied. "I only wish we could've got here first. There's no way - TURN!" You turn as your opponent lunges out of a crouch, a curved dagger flashing. You reach out. The dagger pierces clean through your hand, becoming lodged in the flesh. You lock arms. You struggle for control. "No ... hard ... feelings ... eh, [us-firstname]?" your opponent grunts. The pain is extraordinary. But you're used to pain, and your opponent is weak. You're the one who traveled here in person, as a person, after all. "One of many differences between us -" you feel the knife rend your flesh as you strive for balance. You let go completely. The blade slides free, leaving a fresh stigmata in your palm. Capitalising on good fortune, your opponent drives the blade into your sternum. A better fighter would've slashed your throat rather than drive it into more flesh. "- you don't feel anything at all." You punch your opponent in the teeth. They drop like a sack of rocks. The astral sings in frustration. Light pours from your opponent's mouth, breaking it wide open. Ignoring the pain, you remove the dagger, toss it far into the ether. "Take the bridge!" says a voice in your ear. "While it's weakened! Now!"

name: 79AU_Bridge5
title: The bridge, part 5
desc:
The exterior of 79 AU finishes its preparations. The golden threads are woven into the final form, its outstanding patterns tied off.

One of its passengers assumes command, and the station is fully operational.

A full third of the sphere has become an enormous transmission array extending three times its diameter. Already primed, it fires a burst of energy, an analogue of light not visible from the crushing Baryonic depths below. Out of the barrel it is centimetres wide, widening conically a few degrees. It is aimed at one star in the night sky. 

Faster than light, the burst arrives at Sol ahead of itself, the arc flared wide enough to encompass the eight major planetoids and much else besides. It passes through the local matter without interaction, save for a few million tiny hits clustered around the orbital bodies. In these it achieves an astonishingly dense rapport.

The burst avoids Earth, flowing around it as a river would a rock.

The burst travels for a further 79 AU past its target. It diffuses upon the interstellar medium without effect, two seconds before it is fired.

Another passenger takes the bridge, ousting the first. The array prepares to fire a second shot.

All this is known to you, but you are concerned with other matters. For example -

name: 79AU_Bridge6
title: The bridge, part 6
desc: - elsewhere you hear a voice saying "Terrain, Terrain, Terrain", and a familiar sound, the rapid beeping of the NAV Station. It accelerates until the separate sounds converge in one high pitched alarm, the dumb digital mind wailing as it contends with the distance travelled - - you are still on -

name: 79AU_Bridge7
title: The bridge, part 7
desc: You lift your head to feel the bluster of trade winds brisk and warm on your cheek. Your vessel has reached the end of the delta, thrust onto a distemperate sea, blue and grey in the morning light. Comes the question: Where away? It is yours to answer.

name: 79AU_DeadUniverse1
title: Watch
desc: Earth et al is roughly ten light-hours away. Five not-light hours after you start the journey, you stop receiving comms chatter from Sol. Not all at once. Your information has to get here the old-fashioned way. Traffic in some Neptunian buoys stops flowing except for routine pings, nodes in the network chattering back and forth about machine things on an empty line. Many minutes later, from your perspective, it happens at Titan, at Jupiter, and so on, until hours later the System is nothing but dead air. The ships are still there. The stations are still there. The lights are on, but nobody's home.

name: 79AU_DeadUniverse2
title: Continue
desc:
Your ship limps back to Sol for another span of weeks. You are as glued to the scopes on the way back as you were on the way out.

The system is silent. Ships on Brachistochrone trajectories never finish them, spiralling the sun in crazy arcs, doomed to fall between the planets for the next billion years. Hundreds of ships make planetfall, funeral pyres streaking across the skies of Mars and Venus and Titan. At least two of the major ports become clouds of debris, docking attempts that should have aborted. Hangzhou is the only one to remain totally unscathed. Is automated systems assume control of incoming traffic, an emergency feature the station long denied it possessed.

Throughout weeks of carnage and aimless destruction eclipsing all solar history hitherto, you pick up no S.O.S., no distress calls, not even any complaints or arguments over who was at fault.

name: 79AU_DeadUniverse3
title: Return
desc:
K-LEG looks pretty much the same as you left it. The derelict graveyard has a handful of new, unlicensed headstones. Some of them might need intervention within a year to avoid a nasty collision, but until then everything seems fine ticking over. Whatever contingencies the station planned for, and this was certainly not one of them, the automated systems have handled it.

You coast in to dock as you always have. Ignoring the warnings, you override the clamps. You'll have to fix that. Perhaps you can take the Harbormaster's codes from his quarters.

The docks are quiet and empty for the first time in your life. The air is cool, almost cold, a feat never achieved by the long suffering environmental team. As you stroll past familiar haunts, the unattended kiosks and crew lounges and vending machines and dorms, you find the floors littered with objects that had been held by your former colleagues until the instant they disappeared into thin air. The usual culprits are PDAs and rotting food, power tools, an extra garment or two. They had no idea. They never knew it.

You watch the footage in Station Security, more for something to do than for enlightenment. The clips are uniform, almost boring. In one frame the station is teeming with life. In the next frame it is not. The PDAs float like an afterthought. Everything sets course for 1036 Ganymed below, eventually to be intercepted by the station floor.

name: 79AU_DeadUniverse4
title: Dead Universe
desc:
You are the last and only human. Did Nietzsche conceive of the ubermensch having to feed themselves, use the bathroom, clean their clothes, shave? Does the last man brush his teeth? These needs demand your attention. Some you address out of habit. Others slip now that they're not for anyone.

This station, any station, anywhere you can go, houses more material wealth than one person could ever hope to attain or exhaust. It is yours by default.

You have an embarrassment of riches, a freedom surplus. You can go anywhere, do anything. All you have lost is the observation of others. Whether that is a win or a loss is entirely, solely, your opinion.

name: 79AU_Ose1
title: President Ose in Room 208
desc:
You wheel yourself into the elevator and take it to the second floor. There, a long hallway stretches out and presents six doors, each of them illuminated from above by light fixtures casting a dim orange glow. At the end of the hall there is a final door, and it is ajar. 

Your chair struggles against the carpet. Pushing yourself down the hallway the only noise you hear is the occasional creak of the metal straining against your effort. 

The elegant label on the final door reads '208'. It's already open, which suggests an invitation or a disaster.

name: 79AU_Ose2
title: Enter Room 208
desc: The room is beautifully appointed, with every object carrying the certainty of taste emboldened by infinite resources. The carpet is an emerald green with notes of golden filigree. Plants and drapery climb the walls. The rest of the space is populated with low slung, blonde wood furniture in organic shapes, many of them topped with upholstery in earthy, terracotta tones. You're trying to place the fragrance (sandalwood?) when you see him, a lithe figure sitting near a bookcase and a bonsai tree, one leg crossed above the other. His left hand balances a book in the crevice between his legs and his right rests on an end table near a tumbler full of what you assume is whiskey. The man is wearing a silk kimono tessellated with a pattern of cranes. You're so fascinated by the design that it takes you a moment to notice that he has the head of a black panther. His yellow eyes glance up at you over his glasses, expectantly. "I'm sorry," you stammer. "I'm looking for ..." "Ose," he says. "Great President Ose, apparently. Ruler of thirty legions? Although I've not met them yet. And you are ...?" "[us-firstname]," you say. "Not as exciting as my name, but we can't all be so lucky," Ose says, and closes the book. "Are you from here?" "It's my first time in the hotel." "No, no, not here. Here," Ose says, and makes a broad gesture with both hands. "Oh. Yes?" "I see. I'd ask you to take a seat, but ..." He nods towards your wheelchair. Suddenly feeling like a bad house guest, you roll your chair closer to his, hoping the spot you choose doesn't damage the immaculate feng shui. "A human, then," Ose says, and swirls an ice cube in his glass with a long forefinger. "I've been reading about you. Your kind has quite the imagination. Authors of such varied and exotic worlds. Tell me, why are there so many kings?" "I don't know what you mean." "I've just yet to come across a story that doesn't involve some kind of hierarchy," he says, and tosses the book away in disgust. "Even the heroes are peasants. At least they start that way. Before they become kings." You have no idea what to say. You find yourself falling into his voice. The sonorous and melodic timbre suggests pride for the old world along with fascination with the new. Plus, you must remind yourself again, he's got a bespectacled cat head. "Tell me about Earth," Ose says. "I've never been," you tell him. "A paradise, it seems. Positively teeming with life. Trout in the brooks, birds in the sky. Clouds of gnats. Innumerable microscopic herds of, what did I read...waterbear?" "Not anymore," you say. "Oh, don't be so grim! It's true you've nearly ruined the place. Such a shame. All that grubby infighting. Not the kind of thing a king can solve, unfortunately. But that lesson is hard won. Usually over far more generations than your kind has under their collective belts."

name: 79AU_Ose3
title: Who could solve the infighting, then?
desc:
"It's a good question. The right one," Ose says. "Truthfully, that kind of thing has a way of working itself out after a time. Assuming, you know. The babies aren't strangled in their cribs."

"Is that what we've done? Strangled ourselves?"

"I haven't decided yet," he says. "Perhaps we'll know by the time I finish this drink."

name: 79AU_Ose4
title: Question his appearance
desc:
"Why are you, um..." you think for a minute. "Is your head...?" Still nothing. 

"I should be asking you! I wouldn't think too much about it. Suffice it to say that new worlds come with altered contexts. This one is yours, believe it or not. A very old one. But human nevertheless. Does it frighten you?" he asks.

You don't know what to say.

"No," he muses. " You don't seem the type."

name: 79AU_Ose5
title: Request a drink
desc:
"Of course!" Ose says, and rises to his feet. "Where are my manners?"

Several bottles sit atop a mirrored sideboard between the bookshelf and a large, curtained window. Ose busies himself there as he continues speaking.

"I've never been good at these," he says. "First Contacts. I always find myself bored by the big picture and respond by fixating on the tiniest of details. Here."

He passes you a brown spirit in a short glass tumbler with a single ice cube. 

You take a drink, confirming your suspicion. Whiskey. Real whiskey, even.   

"Crown something, according to the label," Ose observes. "And I'll admit to having never tasted anything like it. Cheers," he says, and raises his glass before sitting down again.

name: 79AU_Ose6
title: Compliment the room
desc:
"Beautiful, isn't it?" Ose says. "Our host presented a range of options. Eras, styles, motifs. Mid century modern leaped out. 20th Century, I should say. Well before our time. What did you think of our host?"

"Joakim? He was...accomodating."

"Yes. That part doesn't change. An entire species whose sole purpose is just that: obsequious accommodation. Rather pitiful."

name: 79AU_Ose7
title: How did you find us?
desc:
"I didn't, I'm ashamed to say. I was following someone else. The much-too-free spirits in Room 103. We don't get along, but they have a knack for turning up new friends that I find useful. They keep wondering why I show up when they do. I'm beginning to wonder whether they have the capacity to realize I've been doing it on purpose."

"How did they find us?"

"You'd have to ask them. As far as I can tell they just like to wander."

name: 79AU_Ose8
title: Enough. What do you want?
desc:
"It's more about what you want, I'm afraid," Ose says, then looks at his nails. They're perfectly manicured, and filed nearly to a point.

"How so?"

"How to put this? You are the first. The vanguard. More of an outrider, really, to preserve the metaphor."

"The first to do what?"

"To come here. To meet another. The Great Cosmic Handshake. We all had one, otherwise we wouldn't be here."

"Did you have one?"

"No, no ..." He waves the question away and takes a delicate sip of his drink. "That was eons ago. You're early to the party, relatively speaking. Must be that special human ambition I've been reading about."

"What does it mean to be first?"

"Ah. That's a privilege, isn't it." Ose leans forward, points a long finger at you. "It means you, my friend, are temporarily in possession of a heretofore hidden knowledge. You and you alone. I'm jealous, really. Discovering such knowledge is the sole purpose of my kind."

"Why?"

Ose stands up and indulges in a long, languid stretch before walking to the bookshelf. He runs a finger along the spines of the volumes there.

"Suppose we return to all those kings for a moment."

"Do we have to?"

"It appears to be your highest aim. Power over others. But in all those stories, can you recall even one happy king?"

You think for a moment.

"What I...what we offer isn't power over others. Such power is a trap, in the best of cases. We offer power over the self. No, that's not right. Still feels hierarchical. Even your language is bound by ideologies of domination. We offer power from the self. A kind of...congruency. Within, but gained from without."

name: 79AU_Ose9
title: What are you again?
desc: Ose lets out a frustrated sigh. "If you're asking after my shape, this might help." Ose scans the books and pulls a decaying tome from among them. He tosses it over to you. It lands in your lap with a painful thud. "The ... I can't pronounce this," you stammer. "Pseudomonarchia Daemonum," Ose says. "Not a fan of 16th Century grimoires I see. Neither was I, until I got here. I didn't choose my shape any more than you did. You'd do well to keep that in mind."

name: 79AU_Ose10
title: You didn't answer my question. What do you want?
desc:
"I want you to stop pretending. Pretending that you're some hapless bystander on the banks of time, watching as the currents pass you by. I'd like you to step into the river."

"Is that what you did?" you ask.

"Of course! Did, and do. It's the only true safety. You'll hear plenty of complaints about our kind, but nobody can say we aren't the agents of our own fortune."

"So that's what you're offering? Safety."

"It's the only promise I'll make."

name: 79AU_Elevator2
title: Return to the elevator
desc:
The elevator readmits you, the chair jolting uncomfortably as you cross the gap.

You have perfect recall of Joakim's information. Where do you want to go?

name: 79AU_Ose11
title: Take your leave
desc:
"This has been ... edifying," you say. You begin to wheel your chair towards the door.

"So soon?" Ose asks. "We were just beginning to come to an understanding."

You're not so sure about that.

"I'm not so sure about that," you say. "But I appreciate the hospitality."

Ose offers no reply. Just a long stare through narrowed eyes as you exit the apartment and wheel yourself back to the elevator.

As the platform climbs to your floor, you think back to what President Ose was trying to tell you. Despite the chasms of misunderstanding, the conversation carried with it a vapor of significance that is already evaporating. You have the feeling that you'd better grasp it quickly, because soon it will be gone forever.

name: 79AU_Night11
title: The Players
desc:
Opposite you is President Ose, now wearing a striking velvet dinner jacket in a rich burgundy hue. You meet his yellow eyes and find nothing there."

"Players may now select a partner," says Joakim. "Provided the partner is willing."

name: 79AU_Ose12
title: I like the sound of the other guys
desc:
"I don't doubt it," Ose says. "It's a seductive idea, moving to and fro without aim, guided by nothing more than desire. Motes floating on the solar winds. Sounds quaint."

"It does."

"I know your kind has that impulse in them. Here and there."

"What impulse?"

"Hedonism. Pleasure as the primary good. Joy as the telos," Ose holds up his empty glass. "Another drink?"

"You sound skeptical," you say.

"Not at all. I'm quite certain, actually."

"Certain of what?"

"That I'd rather be the wind than the mote," Ose replies.

name: 79AU_Ose13
title: Isn't that selfish?
desc:
"Yes," Ose says. "Although, no. Not in the pejorative sense. I'm not sure you have a word for it. Imagine a selfishness that expands. Imagine yourself elevated, beyond. Alone, yes. We all are. Surely you've noticed that. But...untethered."

"Is all your kind untethered?"

"We are, in fact. Eventually. We live and learn and when we've matured to a certain age we just ... leave."

name: 79AU_TripOut
title: The Trip Out
desc:
The trip is a long one, and you find yourself wishing the days would pass with the familiar monotony of long haul travel. Instead, your sparing moments of consciousness are haunted with regrets about the world you left behind, the one you had some hand in creating. 

A New World Order, forged in the hungry fire of the last. Entire nationstates leveled in an instant. The old masters dead or dying. You consider who the new masters will be, and no matter how you look at it, the truth is inescapable: you helped them level a shotgun at the body politic, and then they blew off a couple limbs.    

You miss Ben. You'd love to talk to him. You can't believe that in these moments of self reflection, you find yourself longing for the practical evaluations he produced so effortlessly. On particularly dark days, you even miss the condescending pedantry. It's that bad.   

Your unconscious moments are even more disturbing, somehow. The dreams, once relegated to sleep, have begun to invade your waking moments. Every time you close your eyes you see the golden idol, a version of the Colchian sarcophagus rendered in massive scale and looming over your ship like an angry god. 

What's more, the moment your mind slips out of thought and into patterns of default, you hear the chorus of church bells, the eerie tintinnabulation giving way to a vision of infinite black expanse punctuated by glowing purple nodes in an ever swelling network, each point in the system expanding in logarithmic fractal patterns so vast as to silence what's left of your rational mind.

After all this, you've become a ragged ghost of your former self. Food and sleep present themselves as foreign concepts, crude sources of a nourishment you find better met by long contemplation of the infinite sparkling network that returns to you in vision.

Staring out at the endless and somehow expanding plane of purple nodes, you're struck by the certainty that time has only ever been a side effect of distance, of the velocities necessary to close said distance, a quaint but useful epiphenomenon that managed to confound your species for far too long. 

After all, the very voyage you're on now would have been unthinkable before the development of the Epstein drive powering your ship. Under previous outmoded technologies of thrust, it would take months, years to travel from where you were only days ago. So what of those years? Gone. Obliterated by speeds that previous generations could have only dreamed of.  

"Here to there," you keep saying, often aloud. "Once here. Now there."
